name: Creation ex nihilo
plain_explanation: The doctrine that God made the universe out of absolutely nothing, rather than shaping some pre-existing raw material, as older Greek thought had assumed.
precise_definition: The doctrine, taught in the Old Testament and defended by Augustine against Manichaean and Greek views, that God created substance itself, not merely order and arrangement imposed on eternal, pre-existing matter.
why_it_mattered: It marks a decisive break from Greek metaphysics, where God is an artificer working on eternal matter, and it forces the question of what, if anything, existed 'before' creation -- the problem that leads directly into Augustine's theory of time.
historical_origin: Rooted in Genesis; defended by Augustine as a requirement of Christian orthodoxy against both the Manichaeans and residual Greek assumptions.
examples: Augustine's rejection of the Manichaean objector who asks why God did not create the world sooner
objections: The Greek philosophical view that creation out of nothing is impossible, which recurred in Christian times and, Russell notes, led toward pantheism
competing_positions: Plato and Aristotle's view of God as artificer shaping eternal matter
Pantheism (later fully developed by Spinoza), which denies any real distinction between God and the world
influence_on_later_thinkers: Became settled Christian orthodoxy; the alternative view recurred among mystics, who, Russell notes, have historically found it hard to stay orthodox because they resist placing the world wholly outside God.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly theological; underwrites Augustine's argument that Genesis, not Greek metaphysics, must govern Christian cosmology.
